steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The lighthouse at Blackstone Point was never entirely dark. Even when the lantern was snuffed at dawn, when the great lens was still and the sea lay flat as hammered pewter, a faint glow clung to the stones, as if a century of light had soaked into them.

Elias Morrow had tended that light for forty-two years.

He rose each day before the gulls began their bickering, brewed his coffee black and strong, and climbed the iron spiral with the same slow, deliberate pace he had used when his hair was still the color of wet coal instead of salt. The stairs complained now, but then, so did his knees. They had grown old together, the keeper and his tower.

On most mornings, the routine was ordinary: trim the wick, polish the glass, check the mechanism, log the weather—visibility three miles, light southerly wind, seas calm. Yet Elias knew the sea had a talent for surprising a man the moment he decided things were ordinary.

It was in late autumn, on a morning as gray as unbaked bread, that the fog came.

It rolled in from the horizon like a slow, silent army, swallowing the last clear line of sky and sea. One moment, Elias could see the faint shape of the mainland cliffs; the next, the world ended ten yards from the rocks. He could hear the ocean still—its steady breath against the island’s ribs—but it sounded farther away, as though he’d been lifted into a cloud.

He lit the lamp early.

The familiar click of the mechanism, the faint whoomph of the flame catching, the gradual flare into steady brilliance—all of it calmed the old itch of unease that fog always brought him. He’d seen too many wrecks in his time, too many splintered hulls and broken crates and once, a child’s doll, one glass eye staring up at him from the weed-choked tide line.

He made his entry in the logbook. Date. Time. Weather: dense fog; horn sounding every thirty seconds. He paused, pen hovering, then added: Visibility almost nothing.

The horn bellowed, a mournful sound that seemed to bounce around inside the fog and come back lonelier.

Hours passed. Shapes came and went in the mist—nothing human, only the suggestion of wings, the flit of a shadow, the brief illusion of movement where there was nothing. Elias brewed more coffee, ate half a stale biscuit, and told himself he did not hear voices in the fog.

Near noon, he heard the first distant thrum.

It was a sound felt as much as heard—a low vibration that tickled his bones. Ship’s engine, he thought. He went up again, though he had checked everything twice already. The light swept in its slow, patient circle, a bright blade cutting through wool.

The engine note grew clearer, closer.

Elias stepped out onto the narrow gallery encircling the lantern room and gripped the cold rail. The wind had died away to almost nothing; the horn’s moan felt enormous in the stillness. Somewhere out there, beyond the wall of white, a ship was moving blind.

He remembered, all at once, another fog, thirty years before. A freighter that did not answer the horn. The sickening sound of metal ripping open on rock. The cries that came afterwards.

Elias squinted into the blankness. “You hear me,” he muttered to the unseen vessel. “You see me.”

The engine grew louder, then faltered, then surged again. Too close. He could feel it now, a vibration through the rock itself.

He checked the lamp again though he knew it was burning clean and strong. The lens turned, steady as a heartbeat. The horn sounded and sounded, a desperate call: Here. Here. Here.

Then he saw it—a faint ghost of a shape in the fog, dark and uncertain, sliding across the line of his light.

“Hard to starboard,” he whispered, as though his words could cross that wet void and find a helmsman’s ear.

The shape swelled, became the looming suggestion of a bow. Elias’s hands tightened on the rail until the bones ached. Another blast from the ship’s horn answered his own, so loud he felt it in his chest like a blow. He could hear shouted orders now, robbed of words by the fog.

The ship emerged, a great metal wall passing not two hundred yards from the rocks, water boiling white against her sides. For a breathless instant she seemed to drift sideways, hunting for purchase; then she swung, obedient to her own momentum and whatever frantic hands guided her, and slipped past Blackstone Point like a ghost refusing to touch the living world.

Elias exhaled only when her stern faded back into the gray and her engine beat began to recede.

He stood there for a long time, listening to the diminishing thrum, to the horn’s steady call, to his own blood in his ears. The fog did not lift, but something in him eased. The light had done its work.

That night, with the fog still pressed against the windows like damp cotton, he sat at the small wooden table beside the stove and opened a fresh page in the logbook.

“1130 hours,” he wrote. “Dense fog. Large vessel passed dangerously close to Blackstone Point. Light visible; horn heard. No wreck.”

His hand hesitated, then, on impulse, he added a line he had never written before:

“I am glad I was here.”

He stared at the words, at the curve of his own aging handwriting. The service had sent letters for years now—polite notices about automation, about new systems, about how lighthouses no longer needed keepers. Blackstone was old, remote, stubborn as a molar that refused to loosen, but even stubborn things gave way eventually.

He imagined the tower without footsteps on its stairs, without hands to polish its glass. The lamp would still burn; the horn would still sound. Sensors did not tire; machines did not forget to wind. Yet he could not shake the sense that the tower itself would notice the absence—an empty house where something essential had gone out with the furniture.

Outside, the horn cried again, long and low.

Elias closed the logbook, set it aside, and rose. The stairs waited. The lamp needed checking. Somewhere out there the sea turned in the dark, carrying ships and their sleeping crews past the teeth of Blackstone Point.

He climbed, slow and steady, one hand on the rail, the other brushing the cold stone of the inner wall as if in passing greeting. At the top, in the lantern room, the great lens revolved, throwing its measured brilliance into the wet night.

Elias stepped close, the glow catching in the fine lines of his face, and watched the light make its slow, eternal circle.

“My watch isn’t over yet,” he said quietly, to the tower, to the sea, to no one at all.

Outside, the fog pressed in, but the beam went on cutting through it, stroke after stroke, as it had for generations—and, for a while longer yet, under the steady care of a man who believed that sometimes it was enough, and everything, simply to keep the light burning.
